I'd love it, and be extremely grateful, if you could take a look and leave a review!

Chapter 69: Epilogue 1

Summary:

It came in the blink of an eye...

Notes:

Hello! Sorry for the wait but work kind of got a lot worse recently and I'm kind of in hell right now. But not to worry! I will at least get a TFS epilogue chapter out every week, though expect an updated schedule post sometime in one of my socials. Anyways, hope you enjoy the chapter!

(See the end of the chapter for more notes.)

Chapter Text

It came in the blink of an eye.

“Five copper coins! Take it or leave it,” Kadomon said gruffly. The customer huffed but he paid dutifully. Of course he would, despite how much of a salesman he may act, the appa seller was a fair dealer. He wouldn’t scam his customers with bad products, but he won’t them haggle any lower than the common price. He wasn’t an idiot.

The man sighed as he leaned back on his stool.

Despite how annoyed he was by his customers, he was more irritated by how long the day was going. He wanted to go home and be with Raksha and Plum to celebrate his daughter’s birthday but he had to man the appa stand. He had first wanted to take the whole day off but Raksha had recently gotten in contact with her parents again and was wanting to introduce them to their granddaughter finally.

By the time Raksha had sent back a letter, he was already getting ready to join her in moral support but she denied him. Plum being there was necessary, but she wanted to face her past on her own. It saddened him but he understood. Raksha was a strong woman. She was the type to not rely on anyone by default—an aspect of her that he couldn’t help but love and hate. Kadomon reached up to touch his scar and grinned at the memory. Love because it was what attracted him in the first place and hate because it often meant she would face everything by herself.

But that shouldn’t happen anymore, now that they were a family. She shouldn’t have to face her demons alone. She shouldn’t have to face her estranged parents without him, just because she didn’t want to burden him that nonsense. When you loved someone, you should be there with them, no matter the obstacle. At least, that was what Kadomon believed in.

But he had to respect her wishes, no matter how much he wanted to argue against them. Which was why he was at the appa stand today, waiting for the hours to go by before he could see his lovely wife and daughter and celebrate the rest of the day together. He only hoped that the meeting went well, and that Plum finally had a grandma and a grandpa in her life.

“Hm?” Kadomon looked to the side as he saw a familiar doll peak its head out from the corner of his stand, it looked at the appas with a curious eye and with a lot of exaggerated motion. He had to restrain himself from jumping with joy and instead coughed into his hand, “Ya looking to buy, little Missy?”

The doll looked up in surprise before sheepishly trying to hide itself with its little hands. Kadomon smiled at his daughter’s precociousness, “It’s only five copper coins per appa.”

The doll acted like it was in shock before miming a search through its pockets.

“And there is no use haggling!” Kadomon decided to tease her.

The doll put its hands to its face in dismay before appearing downcast and turning around. Kadomon quickly said, “Wait, wait, perhaps I could give you a discount.”

He noticed someone in the background and pointed to them, “If you could convince that beautiful lady to give a lonely man like me a chance, I’ll let ya get fifty percent off the next batch of appas.”

The doll jumped with glee before turning towards the direction he pointed. Kadomon peeked his head around the corner and saw Plum also turned towards that same direction—where Raksha stood, waving her hand. Before his daughter could react, he picked her up in one fell swoop and hugged her tight, spinning her around while saying, “Oops! Too slow! Ya should have been faster than that!”

Plum screamed and giggled with joy as she wrapped her hands around her father’s neck, happy to see him, “Hey Daddy!”

“Hello my little appa pie, how was your special day?”
She smiled even wider, making his heart warm, “It was awesome! I got to meet Grampy! And Grammy! And even Flammy and Grassy!”

Kadomon snorted, “You did, did you? Were they fun? Did you get a ton of presents?”

Plum nodded rapidly, “They were so cool! Grampy baked me tons of cookies while Grammy put me on her shoulders and carried me around! Flammy and Grassy showed me the garden and their secret hiding spots and—”

While Plum rambled on about her day, Raksha snuck up on them, silently telling Kadomon that the meeting had worked out. And that there was a possibility of a second and maybe even third meeting. Hopefully with him there. He was proud of his wife. So damn proud.

He did frown for a moment, making his emotions clear that he still wished she would have asked him to be there. She sighed and nodded, making an expression that clearly showed she did understand. And that in the moment, she did realize his presence would have been better than his absence and that…

Kadomon held his wife’s hand while still holding onto Plum with the other.

It was okay. He didn’t blame her. Her being scared wasn’t her fault. He then wiped the tears that were about to form in her eyes and brought her close.

“—oh and Grammy made me this really good pudding and gave me all of these snacks to take home!”

Kadomon rubbed his nose on Plum’s, “Well, you must be super full after all that eating!”

Plum rubbed his nose back, slapping his cheeks, “Super duper full!”

“Well…I guess you don’t want to go get some of those egg tarts they sell—”

“No! I do! I do, I do, I do—”
“Okay, okay, I guess you got a second stomach after all. Just like your old man!” Kadomon said as he patted his own belly.

Plum giggled, “Daddy is super duper fat!”

Kadomon tried to hide the twitch of his eye, “No, no, daddy is super duper strong!” Kadomon flexed his muscles only for Plum to lean down and punch his stomach hard, making him wince. She then patted it twice.

“Nope!” She nodded to herself, a serious expression on her face. “I checked! It’s soft, so that’s all fat!”

Kadomon tried to hide the pain and instead glanced at his wife.

Who was barely restraining her laughter.

Oh he was going to pay her back for this.

Before he could drag his wife into his daughter’s antics, she started tapping his neck rapidly, “Dad, dad!”

Kadomon was slightly bewildered, “What is it kiddo, ya see something?”

“Look!” She pointed behind him, “It’s Big Brother!”

Big Brother? Plum had no older siblings. He would definitely know if they existed.

He turned to his wife who suddenly had a horrified expression on her face, no longer laughing like she was just previously. Her eyes focused on where Plum pointed. Concerned by his family’s reaction, Kadomon slowly turned to face the—

Suddenly, a wealth of information was blasted into his skull. Memories that should have been there since the beginning, resurfaced. A face that he merely glanced at everyday, became recognizable. And with it, his mind began to think back to where he first saw that particular scary mug.

Nearly a year and a half ago, some dumbass kid that had no money.

And just a few months later, some dumbass kid who now had money and a girl.

And even a little after, a guy who come visit and buy some appas whenever he visited the capital. Sometimes with a woman. Sometimes not. But always wearing that dumb expression on his face. A cheerful smile that was always on his lips whenever he would say hi to Plum and Raksha.

An expression that was absent and replaced with a scowl, as it hung on a wanted poster, a careful depiction of his features that while not exactly perfect, were recognizable to anyone who had met the lad. But with recognition, came understanding.

In the blink of an eye, Kadomon realized what looked so wrong.

“There’s no way…that’s—”

-----------------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

Bordeaux rubbed his temples in frustration. These meetings had become increasingly hellish in the last few months. With the escape of the Archbishop, a number of disturbing issues had sprung up.

For starters, Blue’s increasingly unstable mental condition. Bordeaux won’t say he was the fondest of the effeminate Demi-human. The boy would constantly go against the norm and tip-toe the formalities of the knights at almost every turn. It was frustrating to talk with him as he would speak with such an annoying inflection that was not needed in the least! Bordeaux even asked other Demi-humans if that was normal, and they said no! The boy was just doing it to be annoying!

…But even still, he couldn’t blame the lad for losing his mind because of his Lady’s depreciating physical state. He could never blame a person for going insane when their loved one was on death’s door.

He would be a hypocrite for doing so.

And yet, he had a duty—an obligation—to his kingdom, just as Blue did. They both were people of grand positions that required responsibilities beyond their own selfishness. Bordeaux had suffered. Suffered more than most but less than the greatest. He understood his own worth. His own weakness. It was why he chose to curb his rage, his aggression, to something more fine-tuned. All for the sake of the kingdom he loved. For the kingdom he would die for. And for the kingdom that his loved ones had died for.

Bordeaux would not waver. But he would also not let his own feelings get in the way of a brighter future. Which was why when he asked Russel Fellow and Six Tongues to investigate Blue’s actions and the events that transpired during the Archbishop’s escape, he could only lament their situation even more.

Torture, bribery, and a coalition of knights that had a bone to pick with cultists. He understood. He truly did. No one hated the cult more than him. No one hated Witches more than him. No one hated enemies of the kingdom more than him. But still…they could not act in such a way without reason. Cruelty must be precise and without emotion. He had learned that well during the war and he made use of it countless times.

Which was why this decision came naturally. While Miklotov argued with another sage, in Bordeaux’s hands lay Blue’s dissolvement. Evidence, witnesses, and more. All prepared and funneled to him by Russel Fellow’s sources. Of course, he wasn’t the only one who had investigated: Marcos, Reinhard, and Julius. Those three came up several times from the Six Tongues reports.

Marcos was the first to notice, it seemed that the Knight Commander was preparing full responsibility for his subordinates crimes. The man was honor-bound as always. Someone who was willing to rebuild the knights at a moment’s notice if they were to become corrupted again. No wonder he was so perceptive.

Reinhard and Julius were a conundrum, however. Bordeaux had seen signs that they too were ready to confront their old friend, though he also doubted they would go through with it. It was difficult to separate personal matters from responsibilities. And he would not blame them for wavering due to their past connections.

But then the two had suddenly disappeared, going on a wild goose chase to the fabled Sage’s Tower. It both befuddled Bordeaux and made him curious. Why were they so adamant to go on that expedition together?

And why did the Six Tongues report that the Juukuulius Household was investigating the Archbishop’s whereabouts in Kararagi?

He had much to think on that but that would come after dealing with Blue. The Archbishop was still a problem but it was an external one. He would not let the internal molds in the kingdom, fester and destroy all that his countrymen had worked so hard to build. They had changed this kingdom for the better. Transformed their foreign affairs from hostile to negotiable. Suppressed rebel forces that could destabilize the crown. Found short and long -terms solutions when the Royal Family had all perished.

They had adapted and survived from every crisis and he would not let this one mistake—weaken its foundations.

Blue would survive. While outwardly, Lugunica would say that Blue was on an extended sabbatical. In actuality, Felix would most likely spend the rest of his days exiled. At least, once his Lady’s life had expired. He would give the boy that saving grace. But no more. To grossly misuse his comrades hatred and contempt for his own means of revenge, was no better than betraying all that the kingdom stood for. Especially if it was done without good reason. And revenge…was no good reason.

It did not bring you happiness. Nor retribution. Just quiet longing.

Bordeaux would not have such idiocy persist. No more.

Once Miklotov was done with his speech, they would soon move onto the matter of the Archbishop. From there they would shift topics to those related, such as Felix Argyle. And at that point, Bordeaux would make his move.

Bordeaux leaned back in his chair and sighed. If nothing, he would pray for the boy. Pray that he would one day find peace, even though he himself knew there was none.

“Now, let’s move onto the next topic on the agenda,” Miklotov adjusted his glasses and looked at the paper in front of him, “Regarding the matter of the escaped Archbishop, Natsuki Subaru, our current efforts to reclaim the criminal has been wrought with failure. Unfortunately—”

Bordeaux let the words drabble on. He knew when to intervene. It was all a matter of patience. It’s a shame really. The Archbishop of Pride. Who knew that he would have turned out to be actually Na—

Bordeaux’s eyes widened.

Oh.

Within the Sages’ chambers, an uproar sprung from all those in attendance.

Mirroring the uproar that spread all across the kingdom.

-----------------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

“You seem tired lass, you doing well these last few days?”

“…Ram has just not been sleeping well. Thank you for your concern,” she said as she bowed.

The old woman huffed but delved no more into Ram’s personal matters. Perhaps it was clear as day that Ram was suffering but no matter how much she hated the circumstances, she could not speak of such matters. Because why try? It would solve nothing.

She could talk and complain about how her Master—the love of her life—had spent months languishing in agony. Barely a remnant of the man he once was, drinking himself into nothing. Ram would compare it to Otto if it wasn’t for Roswaal’s constant lament. The poor man had given up on life, unlike the merchant. She hated this. Hated how he had suddenly turned for the worse after the Priestella incident. After months of good behavior, he suddenly was struck with an onset of extreme depression that no one could diagnose what for.

It was maddening. Maddening because she couldn’t do anything for him. Just like how she couldn’t do anything for her last family member. That blue haired oni that she had no memories of and yet, the connection was there. They were twins, so even if she could not remember their life together, she could sense her absence. It was frustrating. To have no direction, no semblance of a way to solve her lost sister’s problem.

Ram couldn’t help but hate her uselessness.

…And then that man came. With sharp eyes, a knowing look, and black and white hair, he entered into their abode and brought change. Her Master had been reinvigorated, brought back from the edge. Ram would have been happy if it didn’t feel…odd. As if the man in front of her had both regressed and pushed forward in the same step. No longer did he wear makeup, but his scheming had become more pronounced. He assured her that it was still for the good of the camp, but she couldn’t help but feel doubt.

Why was he contacting so many of his vassals? Calling in favors? Asking for the political situation in the capital? Something was amiss. And Ram was wracked with concern to find out why. And yet, despite all of her efforts, she found nothing. Her Master was being thorough and every action to learn more was rebuffed. It was as if he had not only drawn a line between him and the rest of the mansion—but specifically between him and her.

Roswaal had become just like he once was—back before Sanctuary. And as a result, Ram had obtained her own form of depression.

So much so, she did not argue when her fellow maids forced her to go on a trip to Arlem instead of them, citing that the fresh air would bring some life back into her lungs. Perhaps they were right. Ram needed to keep her head steady. To not falter just because of unexpected changes. There was still a light at the end of the tunnel, and it would do no one any good to give up so easily.

Perhaps her time would come. Opportunities were fleeting but when they came, she could only hope that her timing was good.

Ha.

Ram laughed as she walked back home with groceries in her hands. It was funny. To think that she would be the one to hope for good timing. How lame. If Baru—

…Ram stopped and stared out into space.

Her hands began to shake. The bags of supplies in her hands dropped to the floor.

And without even processing all the information that entered her brain, she began to run.

She ran. And ran.

And ran.

Sprinting with all her might, even as her lungs were about to collapse and her body was begging her to stop. She couldn’t stop running. They made a mistake. A horrible mistake. One that they might never be able to take back.

But more than that, there was someone she needed to see. Someone who had just woken up. Someone who would need her sister. Even if she had failed in everything else, she would not miss this timing.

Not for the end of the world.

And just as Ram arrived, seeing Frederica staring at the mansion absentmindedly, Ram’s own body about to break down, she heard a distant wail from inside the mansion.

And an explosion of ice.

-------------------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

Roswaal was happy.

Well, not exactly. He was honestly, quite anxious. Waiting for someone was something he was used to but to wait without that precious book in his hands—that was a new experience. Ever since Priestella, he had been in a slump. For some reason, almost innately, he understood that any chance of achieving his goal was gone. There was nothing certain in this world that could give him strength. It had burnt up in that fire and while he tried his best to move on, to accept the words of those who defeated him, slowly but surely, he had realized the truth.

His dream was dead.

So he decided to spend the rest of his life, doing nothing. He deserved it. After lifetimes of dedication and hard work, of crimes against humanity, it was the ending befitting for him. To die as a drunk old man, yearning for a woman that was no longer here, while the rest of the world forgot about him. He was tired. A part of him had hope that perhaps there was another way forward, but he had relied so long on the book that there was an overwhelming feeling of acceptance.

Roswaal had lost. Anymore work would only lead to even more failure and precocious dreaming. Perhaps it was slothful, but he had enough of diligence. Just let him die and have all his failures and sins die with him.

It was the best for both the world and his own story.

And then that boy arrived. Or perhaps he should call him an old man, given how his eyes had no spark of youth and his hair and skin were marked with years. Roswaal couldn’t help but laugh at the resemblance. For once in his life, he had met someone who was just like him, in so many ways. Or perhaps, twice in his life.

The recognition, the odd behavior, and his own confession of their previous connection: Roswaal had already figured it out in the first minutes of their reunion, but he had his doubts. Doubts that slowly corroded as he observed the old boy’s movements. And as these doubts died, they were reborn as something entirely more.

Conviction. This was the one he was waiting for. The person his book must have described. In a timeline that no longer existed, where he had failed—all the pieces in his mind began to connect. All of the little inconsistencies, the odd occasions of luck, were not just a system of circumstance but a finely crafted tale woven by an all-powerful puppeteer. In that moment, when the stars finally aligned, Roswaal’s nights of drifting alone under the dark sky would be no longer. For he had a star, shining brighter than he had ever seen, guiding his path once more.

He no longer needed his book. For he had certainty that this old boy would lead him to salvation. Because even though this old boy looked nothing like him. He too was just a man, yearning for a woman who was no longer here.

Roswaal had died again that day, not unlike all of his previous lives. But unlike all of the other Roswaals, this one no longer desired another life. The only he life he wanted was one where he succeeded. Where it was either the achievement of his dream or the total destruction of himself. The cost of victory was dire, but a person could not dare to reach the peaks if they did not risk everything they owned and loved.

Which was why Roswaal made that bet. Win or lose, the old Roswaal would no longer exist. But if he lost…then a new one would rise. Reborn with conviction.

Following only the black star, that would burn down the world for his Greed.

“Roswaal-sama, is there anything else you would like?” Petra said as she dutifully bowed her head. Roswaal knew this was all fanfare and that the little girl had little loyalty for him. No, her affections lied toward the others in the mansion, but a part of him had a theory that wasn’t the whole story.

Just like with her and just like with everyone else, Roswaal was slowly building the necessary pieces in preparation for when his gambit paid off. It was only humorous to him that for once in his life, he desired to fail more than anything.

“No, that will be all,” Roswaal took a sip of his tea. He smiled. How rebellious. She gave him the worst tea in the cabinet. Unlike Ram who would give him the best of the best. He remembered how Su—

Roswaal blinked. His mind carefully placed all of the missing pieces back into place—their locations already fitted with imagined possibilities that graciously allowed themselves to be replaced with the real ones. His smile became even wider than before and for once, in almost a whole year since he lost.

Roswaal laughed.

“Roswaal-sama? Wh—” Petra paused suddenly, her eyes rattled.

Roswaal couldn’t help but laugh even more. It seemed Gluttonies effects were different for every person. But its destruction was immediate. Unlike the soft disappearance of their names, the return was calamitous and loud. A cacophony of memories that rendered your mind asunder, trying to cope with the various timelines of thought that you once believed were real.

In that same moment, Roswaal heard a scream. And he felt not only his instincts rise but also his magical defenses. It was good to be prepared and he had expected his outcome.

But not the ending of this bet. No. Roswaal had expected himself to win. For his bet to end with his final victory and eventual death. But surprisingly, and to his own satisfaction, Roswaal had failed.

And now was the beginning of a new story.

“Petra-chan, do oblige me for a moment and stay close,” Roswaal jumped over the desk and grabbed the little maid. “I do believe it is time for us to leave.”

He did not blame the child for having tears in her eyes. For he too was crying, though his was sourced from joy, rather than grief.

Being born again always required tears.

------------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

Frederica Baumann was concerned.  These past few months have been quite dreadful. She could sense that everyone was on edge, but she could never pinpoint why. And with the expedition underway—and that unexpected guest—Frederica couldn’t help but feel…dread. Like something awful was about to happen at any moment.

She chuckled to herself.

Perhaps she has become bored from the monotony. Such thoughts are relegated to those with too much time on their hands. They were akin to characters from her novels where the protagonist had a premonition right before delving deep into a conspiracy of unknown proportions. It was laughable to think such things.

Life was never like that. While her life was exciting at times, the monotony was preferrable. Rather than a sudden turn of events, she would rather life become a perpetual state of boredom. Where no one could get hurt, and everyone could live their lives in peace.

Still, one could only dream. Though some dream bigger than others. She was not one of them. No. Not at all. But she did respect those who did. Such as N—

Frederica blinked.

And everything made sense.

As she turned back to the mansion that was once filled with life and had slowly deteriorated over the months. Despite looking as it always was, inside, there was a festering hole that could not be quenched. For months, no one could tell what it was nor who it was that was missing. But innately they all knew.

You couldn’t just take someone integral out and expect everyone to move on. No. Life wasn’t like that. These holes left behind, tear away at the foundations, and rip you apart from within. Like a hidden plague, that has no cure. Building, crumbling, cracking. Each brick, each layer, rotting away as time corrupts. You may not even notice. Because at first, the absence is just that—nothing. Nothing was there. You could see nothing. You felt nothing. You breathed nothing. But you couldn’t live with nothing. Even if you tried all you could, you couldn’t ignore it forever. When everything becomes brittle and destitute, all you can do is watch.

As the foundation you so lovingly built, explodes.

“NOOOOOOOOOO!!!!” Emilia’s screams were the precursor to the end.

And just as  Frederica heard footsteps behind her—the recognizable rhythm of Ram and the wind from her master’s flight above. Frederica did not turn around as she watched the mansion turn into a miniature glacier—wood and debris sent flying as a giant shard of ice was erected over Emilia’s room.

Nor did she turn around when Ram screamed with despair and rushed forward. Or when her master carefully put Petra down beside her and in the same movement, stopped a rabid Ram from breaking through the front door.

With a quick few sentences, “Do not worry. Her room was secured with spells after the last incident. She would be the safest person in this whole mansion, even if it was burnt down and destroyed with a dragon’s breath,” Ram calmed herself, though still antsy given her increased heartrate.

Roswaal then walked past Frederica and the others, tiptoed his way to the doors, and leisurely opened one, gesturing them to enter, “Come now. There is much to do. Much to clean up. This incident cannot be just swept under the rug.”

Frederica did not turn around as Petra sullenly and despondently followed orders and Ram walked briskly forward.

She watched the others backs, as each one stood differently. One marked with despair, one marked with regret, and the last with purpose.

After some time, she took took a deep breath and marched forward herself. It was the only way they had left.

-----------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

As cold air wafted into her room, a frigid icicle burst through the wall, right over her bed. Even though such an object was precariously hung over her body, the magical spells that perforated all over the room would keep her safe and sound.

For so long, she had been in a deep slumber. And yet, despite it all, she couldn’t help but remember. Remember her last moments, her last prayer, to the hero that had saved her life.

The hero that always saved her life.

And as her eyes fluttered open, as her time once again moved forward, she could only look back to the outside world.

And blink.

--------------------------

It came in the blink of an eye.

When Otto awoke, he didn’t know what he expected to see. Maybe death. Or Heaven. Or Hell. He definitely deserved that last one.

But no, the last thing he expected to see was an old friend. Right there, standing beneath the stars in a moonlit sky—in the middle of this tumultuous desert. Where nothing but carnage and danger laid beneath, he was there. Changed. But not forgotten.

Not anymore.

With tears beginning to form under his eyes and a maelstrom of emotion gripping his gut, all he could say was, “…Natsuki-san—Urgh!”

“SHUT THE FUCK UP!” A very angry and beautiful woman with white hair screamed as she kicked him back to the ground.

Otto groaned in agony.

Perhaps this was a fitting end.
